title: Redox reactions
outcomes: Reduction potentials and the direction of electron flow
Nernst equation and free energy from ΔE
Redox cofactors: NAD, NADP and flavins

summary.overview: Cells get most of their energy by stripping electrons from reduced fuels and passing them, step by step, to O2. Each redox pair has a reduction potential; electrons flow from lower to higher E, and the difference (ΔE) sets the free energy available.

sections.heading: Redox basics
points: Oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain. They always occur together (a conjugate redox pair, e.g. NAD⁺/NADH).
Many biological oxidations are dehydrogenations: 2 electrons leave as a hydride ion (:H⁻) plus a proton.
Reduced organic compounds (fuels) are the electron donors; O2 is the final acceptor in aerobic organisms.

sections.heading: Reduction potential and electron flow
points: The standard reduction potential E′° measures a pair's affinity for electrons: the higher (more positive) the E′°, the greater the affinity.
Electrons flow spontaneously from the pair with lower E′° to the pair with higher E′°.
Reference values: NAD⁺/NADH −0.320 V; FAD/FADH2 −0.219 V; pyruvate/lactate −0.185 V; cytochrome c +0.254 V; ½O2/H2O +0.816 V.

sections.heading: Nernst equation and ΔG
points: Nernst: E = E′° + (RT/nF) ln([electron acceptor]/[electron donor]). At 25 °C, E = E′° + (0.059/n) log([ox]/[red]).
ΔE′° = E′°(acceptor) − E′°(donor), and ΔG′° = −nFΔE′° (F = 96.5 kJ/V·mol).
A positive ΔE gives a negative ΔG. NADH → O2: ΔE′° = 1.136 V, so ΔG′° ≈ −219 kJ/mol, enough to make several ATP.

sections.heading: Redox cofactors
points: NAD⁺ and NADP⁺ (pyridine nucleotides) accept a hydride; they bind loosely and move between enzymes.
NADH mostly carries electrons from catabolism to the respiratory chain; NADPH supplies reducing power for biosynthesis.
NADH absorbs light at 340 nm (NAD⁺ does not), so dehydrogenase reactions are followed spectrophotometrically, e.g. in clinical enzyme assays.
FAD and FMN (flavins) are bound tightly and can transfer one or two electrons, which lets flavin oxidases use O2.

keyTerms.definition: Electron donor and its oxidised form, e.g. NADH/NAD⁺.
Affinity of a redox pair for electrons under standard conditions at pH 7.
E = E′° + (RT/nF) ln([ox]/[red]), the potential at actual concentrations.
96.5 kJ/V·mol, the charge of one mole of electrons.
:H⁻, a proton with two electrons, transferred to NAD(P)⁺.
Enzyme that oxidises a substrate by removing hydrogen (H⁺ + hydride).
Enzyme with tightly bound FAD or FMN.

examTips: Electrons flow towards the MORE POSITIVE E′°.
ΔE′° = E(acceptor) − E(donor); then ΔG′° = −nFΔE′° (watch the sign and n).
NADH is for energy (catabolism); NADPH is for biosynthesis.
The A340 of NADH is the basis of many laboratory enzyme assays.

questions.stem: In the reaction ethanol + NAD⁺ → acetaldehyde + NADH + H⁺, which species is oxidised?

options.text: Ethanol, which loses two electrons (a hydride plus a proton)
options.why: Oxidation is loss of electrons; ethanol is the electron donor (reducing agent).

options.text: NAD⁺, which gives up electrons to ethanol as it becomes NADH
options.why: NAD⁺ gains electrons, so it is reduced to NADH.

options.text: Acetaldehyde, which is formed by removing hydrogen from NADH
options.why: Acetaldehyde is the product of the oxidation, not the species being oxidised.

options.text: No species, because it is a hydrolysis in which water is added
options.why: Electrons are transferred, so it is a redox reaction.

questions.stem: When a dehydrogenase oxidises a secondary alcohol to a ketone using NAD⁺, how are the two electrons removed?

options.text: As a hydride ion (:H⁻) transferred to NAD⁺, with a proton released to the solvent
options.why: NAD⁺ accepts the hydride (2 e⁻ + 1 H⁺); the second H⁺ goes into solution.

options.text: As two separate free electrons released into the water, where NAD⁺ later picks them up
options.why: Free electrons do not exist in solution; they move with H atoms or between cofactors.

options.text: As molecular hydrogen gas (H2), which diffuses away from the enzyme's active site
options.why: Dehydrogenases don't release H2 gas.

options.text: As an oxygen atom added to the alcohol carbon, which turns the C–OH group into C=O
options.why: That would be an oxygenase reaction, not a dehydrogenation.

questions.outcome: Reduction potentials and the direction of electron flow
questions.stem: What does a highly positive standard reduction potential (E′°) tell you about a redox pair?

options.text: Its oxidised form has a high affinity for electrons, so it tends to be reduced
options.why: Higher E′° means a stronger electron acceptor, e.g. O2/H2O at +0.816 V.

options.text: Its reduced form readily donates electrons, so it is a strong reducing agent in cells
options.why: Good donors have very negative E′°, e.g. NADH at −0.320 V.

options.text: It cannot take part in biological reactions, because it holds its electrons too tightly
options.why: O2, the most positive biological pair, is the final acceptor of respiration.

options.text: It reacts quickly, because a large potential means a low activation energy
options.why: E′° is thermodynamic; it says nothing about rate.

questions.outcome: Reduction potentials and the direction of electron flow
questions.stem: E′° values: NAD⁺/NADH −0.320 V; fumarate/succinate +0.031 V. Under standard conditions, which way do electrons flow?

options.text: From NADH to fumarate, producing NAD⁺ and succinate
options.why: Electrons move from the lower (more negative) E′° to the higher one.

options.text: From succinate to NAD⁺, producing fumarate and NADH
options.why: That is uphill (ΔE′° negative), so it is not spontaneous under standard conditions.

options.text: There is no flow, because both values are close to zero
options.why: The difference of 0.351 V is substantial.

options.text: From fumarate to NADH
options.why: Fumarate is the oxidised form; it accepts rather than donates electrons.

questions.outcome: Nernst equation and free energy from ΔE
questions.stem: E′° (½O2/H2O) = +0.816 V and E′° (NAD⁺/NADH) = −0.320 V. What is ΔG′° for the oxidation of NADH by O2 (n = 2, F = 96.5 kJ/V·mol)?

options.text: About −219 kJ/mol
About +219 kJ/mol
options.why: A positive ΔE′° gives a negative ΔG′°.

options.text: About −95 kJ/mol
options.why: This subtracts the potentials the wrong way (0.816 − 0.320 = 0.496 V).

options.text: About −110 kJ/mol
options.why: This forgets that n = 2 electrons are transferred.

questions.outcome: Nernst equation and free energy from ΔE
questions.stem: Lactate dehydrogenase uses NADH (E′° −0.320 V) to reduce pyruvate (pyruvate/lactate E′° −0.185 V). What is ΔG′° for pyruvate + NADH + H⁺ → lactate + NAD⁺?

options.text: About −26 kJ/mol, so the reaction is favourable
About +26 kJ/mol, so the reaction is unfavourable
options.why: The acceptor (pyruvate) has the higher E′°, so ΔE′° is positive and ΔG′° negative.

options.text: About −97 kJ/mol
options.why: This adds the magnitudes (0.505 V) instead of subtracting.

options.text: 0 kJ/mol
options.why: The two E′° values differ, so ΔG′° is not zero.

questions.outcome: Nernst equation and free energy from ΔE
questions.stem: In a cell compartment, [NAD⁺]/[NADH] = 10. Using E = E′° + (0.059/n) log([ox]/[red]) with E′° = −0.320 V and n = 2, what is the actual E?

options.text: About −0.290 V
About −0.350 V
options.why: Excess oxidised form makes E more positive, not more negative.

options.text: About −0.261 V
options.why: This forgets to divide by n = 2.

options.text: Exactly −0.320 V
options.why: E = E′° only when [ox] = [red].

questions.outcome: Nernst equation and free energy from ΔE
questions.stem: In the Nernst equation, when does the actual reduction potential E equal the standard value E′°?

options.text: When the concentrations of the oxidised and reduced forms are equal
options.why: The log term is log 1 = 0, so E = E′°.

options.text: When only the reduced form is present in the solution
options.why: Then [ox]/[red] → 0 and E becomes very negative.

options.text: At any concentration, because E is a constant for a pair
options.why: E varies with concentration; E′° is the constant.

options.text: Only at 0 °C, when the RT/nF term is equal to zero
options.why: Temperature affects the RT/nF factor, but the condition is [ox] = [red].

questions.outcome: Reduction potentials and the direction of electron flow
questions.stem: In the respiratory chain, electrons pass from NADH (−0.320 V) through ubiquinone (+0.045 V) and cytochrome c (+0.254 V) to O2 (+0.816 V). Why are they passed in small steps rather than directly to O2?

options.text: Each step releases a manageable share of free energy, which is captured by pumping protons, not lost as heat
options.why: The total ΔG is the same, but stepwise transfer along increasing E lets the cell harvest it efficiently.

options.text: The direct reaction of NADH with O2 would be endergonic, so it needs intermediate carriers to go forward
options.why: NADH → O2 is strongly exergonic (≈ −219 kJ/mol).

options.text: Stepwise transfer makes more total free energy available than the single direct transfer to oxygen would
options.why: Total ΔG depends only on the start and end pairs.

options.text: Electrons flow from a higher to a lower E′°, so they need carriers in descending order
options.why: Electrons flow from lower to higher E.

questions.outcome: Redox cofactors: NAD, NADP and flavins
questions.stem: Serum ALT and AST activities are measured in many veterinary laboratories by following the change in absorbance at 340 nm. What is actually being measured?

options.text: Conversion of NADH to NAD⁺ in a linked dehydrogenase reaction, as only NADH absorbs at 340 nm
options.why: The transaminase product is coupled to an NADH-dependent dehydrogenase, and the fall in A340 tracks the reaction rate.

options.text: The absorbance of the transaminase protein itself, which rises as more enzyme becomes active
options.why: Proteins absorb mainly at 280 nm, and their amount does not change during the assay.

options.text: The absorbance of NAD⁺, which is strongest at 340 nm and increases as the reaction proceeds
options.why: NAD⁺ does not absorb at 340 nm; that is why the assay works.

options.text: Haemoglobin released from red cells damaged by the enzyme, which absorbs strongly at 340 nm
options.why: Haemolysis can interfere with assays but is not what is measured.

questions.outcome: Redox cofactors: NAD, NADP and flavins
questions.stem: Cells keep NAD⁺/NADH and NADP⁺/NADPH as separate pools. What is the main role of each?

options.text: NAD⁺ mainly accepts electrons in catabolism; NADPH mainly donates them for reductive biosynthesis
options.why: A high NAD⁺/NADH ratio favours oxidation; a high NADPH/NADP⁺ ratio favours biosynthesis (e.g. fatty acids).

options.text: They are interchangeable in most enzymes, and are kept separate only so they can be stored in different organelles
options.why: Most dehydrogenases are specific for one or the other.

options.text: NADPH is used only to make ATP in the mitochondria, while NAD⁺ accepts electrons in biosynthesis
options.why: NADPH supplies reducing power for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence.

options.text: NADH is used only in DNA synthesis, while NADP⁺ accepts electrons from glycolysis and the TCA cycle
options.why: NADH feeds electrons into the respiratory chain.

questions.outcome: Redox cofactors: NAD, NADP and flavins
questions.stem: How do flavin cofactors (FAD, FMN) differ from NAD⁺?

options.text: Flavins are tightly bound to their proteins and can move one or two electrons, so oxidases can use O2
options.why: The stable semiquinone form allows single-electron steps; NAD⁺ transfers only a hydride (two electrons).

options.text: Flavins diffuse freely between many dehydrogenases, just like NAD⁺, carrying a hydride ion each time
options.why: Flavins are usually tightly or covalently bound (flavoproteins).

options.text: Flavins cannot accept electrons themselves; they only position the substrate for NAD⁺ to oxidise
options.why: FAD is reduced to FADH2.

options.text: Flavins are inorganic metal ions, such as Fe²⁺ and Cu⁺, that sit in the active site of the enzyme
options.why: They are organic cofactors derived from riboflavin (vitamin B2).

questions.outcome: Nernst equation and free energy from ΔE
questions.stem: For an electron transfer from donor to acceptor to be spontaneous, what must be true?

options.text: E(acceptor) > E(donor), so ΔE is positive and ΔG = −nFΔE is negative
options.why: A positive potential difference drives electrons 'downhill' to the acceptor.

options.text: E(acceptor) < E(donor), so electrons fall from the higher to the lower E
options.why: That gives a negative ΔE and a positive ΔG.

options.text: ΔE must equal zero, so that no energy is lost during the transfer
options.why: ΔE = 0 means equilibrium, with no net flow.

options.text: n must be larger than 2, so that enough electrons move to make ΔG negative
options.why: The number of electrons scales ΔG but does not set its sign.

questions.stem: Why are reduced organic compounds such as fatty acids and glucose described as metabolic fuels?

options.text: Their electrons are removed in oxidation and passed to O2, releasing free energy the cell captures
options.why: Electrons flow from fuels (low E) to O2 (high E), releasing energy along the way.

options.text: They are already fully oxidised, so their carbon atoms can be stored safely without reacting
options.why: Fully oxidised carbon (CO2) has no energy left to release.

options.text: They accept electrons from O2 when they are broken down, which releases free energy as heat
options.why: O2 is the electron acceptor; fuels are donors.

options.text: They contain stored ATP molecules, which are released when the fuel is broken down in cells
options.why: ATP is made from the energy of their oxidation.

flashcards.back: Oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain. The donor is oxidised, the acceptor is reduced.
